summary: Beyond Earth is an interactive and educational website designed to introduce young audiences to the history and importance of NASA’s space missions to the Moon and Mars. The platform addresses the challenge by telling the story of the equipment left behind in these environments, explaining why it was sent, what scientific discoveries it enabled, and its current status. Through accessible texts, images, interesting facts, timelines, and interactive quizzes, the website transforms scientific and historical information into a dynamic and easy-to-understand experience. The project is important because it aims to bring young people closer to science, technology, and space exploration, sparking their interest in knowledge that often goes unnoticed. In addition to preserving the history of these missions, we want to demonstrate that their results continue to contribute to science and help humanity better understand the universe.
details: The challenge addressed by our group was “Abandoned but Not Forgotten: Tales of NASA’s Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars.” The problem becomes evident when we notice the lack of public knowledge and interest in these pieces of equipment, which, despite no longer being operational, represent a history of scientific and technological advances. The audience most affected by this issue is young people, due to the limited availability of interactive and engaging content that facilitates learning and generates interest. Our project, called Beyond Earth, aims to make knowledge more accessible and enjoyable while preserving the legacy of these pieces of equipment. We created an interactive digital exhibition about five missions to the Moon and Mars: Sojourner, Viking, Opportunity, Apollo 15, with its lunar rover, and Apollo 11. The idea was to present a topic full of information in a more interesting way than long pages containing only text, encouraging curiosity and engagement among younger visitors. The website supports two languages: English and Brazilian Portuguese. Visitors can follow the missions through a timeline with six stages, learn about the equipment through images and stories, compare their sizes, explore the orbits on a map, and consult a glossary if they have difficulty understanding any term. We sought to combine learning with entertainment through characters and interactive activities. The robot Nilo narrates the stories, while Elaine guides visitors and provides tips during the minigame. The website also features quizzes to test the knowledge acquired while exploring the missions. We developed our MVP, which consists of a minigame based on space missions, in which correct answers reward users with parts to assemble a virtual explorer robot composed of six pieces. The minigame is only unlocked after the user has explored all the equipment, allowing new attempts in case of incorrect answers and making mistakes part of the learning process. To develop the project, we used information and images provided by NASA on its official websites about the Moon and Mars. For those who wish to learn even more, the Sources section brings together official NASA references, allowing visitors to explore the topics independently. The project was developed using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, without external frameworks, with the assistance of artificial intelligence tools such as OpenAI’s ChatGPT. We used Node.js to perform code and data checks, as well as Git and GitHub to track changes and organize the project files. In the final stage, we used Vercel to host and make our website available online. During development, our team considered the age of the target audience, ease of navigation, the appearance of the pages, and the importance of presenting reliable scientific information in a simple, accessible, and enjoyable way. The project creates value by encouraging young people’s interest in science, technology, and space exploration. We hope to spark the curiosity of future generations and show that learning about science can also be fun. Furthermore, the project has the potential to develop further through partnerships with schools and scientific institutions. We seek partnerships and mentorship to improve our project, expand its reach, and inspire future generations. After all, these pieces of equipment were abandoned, but their stories must not be forgotten.
